questions.q: Define "context clue" and name the four main types taught in Class 11-12 English.
questions.a: A context clue is a hint within the surrounding text that helps deduce a word's meaning. The four main types are: (1) Definition/Restatement, (2) Example/Illustration, (3) Contrast/Antonym, (4) Inference/Tone. A wrong answer (e.g., "looking in a dictionary") reveals the student conflates external resources with internal textual evidence, a habit that fails in unseen-passage exams where dictionaries are banned.

questions.q: In the sentence "The Maharaja was thrilled beyond measure when he killed his first tiger," the phrase "beyond measure" is an idiom. Using only the context of the story's satire, explain what "beyond measure" suggests about the Maharaja's emotional state and the author's attitude.
questions.a: "Beyond measure" literally means extremely, but in this satirical context it suggests the Maharaja's joy is excessive, absurd, and disproportionate — hinting at his hollow vanity. The author uses hyperbole to mock the king's trivial triumph. A student who answers only "very happy" misses the ironic distance and fails to see how vocabulary reveals authorial critique.

questions.q: The text says: "The tiger population became extinct in the forests of Pratibandapuram. Who knows whether the tigers practised birth control or committed harakiri?" Determine the meaning of "harakiri" from context and explain why the author chooses this specific Japanese term instead of "suicide."
questions.a: Context clues: "extinct," "birth control," and the rhetorical question imply self-destruction. "Harakiri" means ritual suicide by disembowelment. The author chooses it for its exotic, violent connotation and dark humor — it elevates the tigers' disappearance to a deliberate, dramatic act, mocking the Maharaja's obsession. A wrong answer like "running away" ignores the death imagery and the satirical tone.

questions.q: Compare the connotations of "vow" (Paragraph III) and "pledge" (not in text, but a synonym). Why does Kalki use "vow" when describing the Maharaja's promise to kill a hundred tigers? How does this word choice interact with the astrologer's prophecy?
questions.a: "Vow" carries solemn, almost religious weight, binding the speaker morally. "Pledge" is more formal/secular. Kalki uses "vow" to heighten the tragic irony: the Maharaja treats a bloodthirsty quest as a sacred duty, while the prophecy frames it as a fatal curse. The word elevates the absurdity, making the eventual death by a wooden tiger a cosmic joke. A student who treats them as interchangeable misses how diction shapes thematic irony.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the word "satyagraha" (Paragraph V) when the dewan's tiger "launched its satyagraha and refused to get out of the car." Does this allusion to Gandhi's non-violent resistance enhance or undermine the story's satire? Justify.
questions.a: It enhances the satire brilliantly. "Satyagraha" evokes moral courage and peaceful protest; applying it to a terrified, passive tiger being dragged to its death creates grotesque irony. It mocks the Maharaja's manufactured heroism by contrasting it with genuine moral resistance. A student who calls it "just a fancy word for refusal" fails to see the intertextual layer that deepens the political satire on colonial and princely power.

questions.q: Write a two-sentence micro-story using the word "suppurating" (from the infection description) that captures the same blend of physical horror and dark irony found in the story's ending.
questions.a: Example: "The dictator's gold-plated throne gave him a suppurating sore where the rusted spring pierced his royal thigh; the wound festered while he signed peace treaties." A strong answer uses "suppurating" correctly (pus-forming) and mirrors the story's pattern: a symbol of power becomes the agent of grotesque downfall. A weak answer uses the word mechanically without irony.
